@luau/global/class.documentation: Refinement and runtime reflection of Luwu classes and objects.

@luau/global/class.fields.documentation:
Returns a table mapping the passed class or object's public fields with their values, as well
as a boolean describing whether the returned map is a 'complete' representation of the
fields available.

This function operates slightly differently on classes and objects. If the passed value
is an object, returns a map of the object's current fields and values. If any field has a
`nil` value, assigns `none` instead of `nil` so the field's name can be stored in the table.
Values in the returned map are shallow clones.

If the passed value is a `class`, all values of the map will be `none`, including those that have
default values. This is because we don't want `class.fields` to unintentionally initialize default values
(which could cause side effects).

@luau/global/class.fields/returns/0.documentation: A map of public fields of the object or class, keyed by field name.

@luau/global/class.fields/returns/1.documentation: Whether the map returned is a complete representation of the object's fields; this will be `true` if the class only has public fields and `false` if the class has any private fields.

@luau/global/class.implements.documentation:
Returns `true` if `o` is an object of a class that implements trait `t`, whether the class lists
`t` after `implements` or gets it through another trait that `needs` it.

If `o` is not an object, returns `false`. Raises a runtime error if `t` is a class rather than a trait
(use `class.isinstance` for classes).

In the type system, this refines `o` to the trait:

```luwu
local function describe(value: unknown): string?
    if class.implements(value, Named) then
        return value.name
    end
    return nil
end
```

@luau/global/class.implements/params/0.documentation: The value you want to test. Anything is accepted here, passing a non-object just causes this function to return `false`.

@luau/global/class.implements/params/1.documentation: The trait you want to check against. Must be a trait.

@luau/global/class.implements/returns/0.documentation: Whether the object `o`'s class implements trait `t`.

@luau/global/class.isinstance.documentation:
Returns `true` if `o` is an object of class `c`.

If `o` is not an object, returns `false`. Raises a runtime error if `c` is not a `class`.

In the type system, you can use this to refine upon an object that could be of one or more classes:

```luwu
type Animal = Cat | Dog
class Cat(name: string, age: number, meows = 2) end
class Dog(name: string, age: number, barks = 3) end

const animal: Animal = get_animal()
if class.isinstance(animal, Cat) then
    print(`found a Cat! {animal.name} with {animal.meows} meows`)
elseif class.isinstance(animal, Dog) then
    print(`found a Dog! {animal.name} with {animal.barks} barks`)
end
```

Since Luwu doesn't support is-a inheritance relationships between classes, you can treat
this as an exact check that an object was instantiated from class `c`.

@luau/global/class.isinstance/params/0.documentation: The object you want to test. Anything is accepted here, passing a non-object just causes this function to return `false`.

@luau/global/class.isinstance/params/1.documentation: The class you want to check against. Must be a `class`.

@luau/global/class.isinstance/returns/0.documentation: Whether the object `o` is an object of class `c.`

@luau/global/class.name.documentation: Returns the identifier name of the class or the class the object is an instance of. Keep in mind this name isn't globally unique, rely on class.isinstance tests instead.

@luau/global/class.name/params/0.documentation: An object or a class you want the name of.

@luau/global/class.name/returns/0.documentation: The identifier name of the class or object.

@luau/global/class.of.documentation: Returns the `class` that `o` is an object of.

@luau/global/class.of/returns/0.documentation: If `o` is an object, then the object's class. Returns `nil` if `o` is not an object.

@luau/global/luwon.documentation:
Reads and writes `.luwon` data files (Luwu Object Notation).

A data file is a list of `const` declarations that ends in `return <value>`. Because reading one never
runs code, it's safe to read a file you didn't write.

```luwu
-- chimera.luwon
const dependencies = {
    json = "1.0.0", -- pinned until 2.0 ships
}

return {
    name = "chimera",
    dependencies = dependencies,
}
```

Read it, change it and write it back. Only the values you changed are rewritten and comments stay where
they are:

```luwu
const manifest = luwon.decode<<Manifest>>(fs.readfile("./chimera.luwon"))
manifest.dependencies.http = "2.0.0"
fs.writefile("./chimera.luwon", luwon.encode(manifest))
```

`require("./chimera")` reads a data file too.

@luau/global/luwon.comments.documentation:
Returns the comments and location of `t[key]`, or `nil` if there are none.

```luwu
const info = luwon.comments(manifest, "dependencies") or return
print(info.above[1].text) -- the comment line above `dependencies = ...`
print(info.after)         -- the comment at the end of its line
print(info.binding)       -- the const it's written with, and that const's comments
```

Without `key`, returns every comment in the file.

Changing the result changes nothing. Use `luwon.setcomments` for that.

@luau/global/luwon.comments/params/0.documentation: A table from a data file.

@luau/global/luwon.comments/params/1.documentation: The key whose comments you want.

@luau/global/luwon.comments/returns/0.documentation: `{ above, after?, location?, keylocation?, binding? }`, or `nil`.

@luau/global/luwon.data.documentation:
Lets a `luwon.reader` build a class that has methods or its own `__init`.

By default the reader passes the call to the constructor and `luwon.encode` writes the object's
fields back. `__todata` and `__fromdata` let the file hold a different shape than the object:

```luwu
class Rect(public min: vector, public max: vector) implements luwon.data
    -- luwon.encode calls this and writes the values it returns between the parentheses, one per slot
    public function __todata(self)
        const size = self.max - self.min
        return self.min.x, self.min.y, size.x, size.y
    end

    -- reader:decode calls this with the values between the parentheses and uses the object it returns
    public function __fromdata(x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number): Rect
        return Rect(vector.create(x, y, 0), vector.create(x + width, y + height, 0))
    end
end

type Layout = { window: Rect }

const layout = luwon.reader({ Rect }):decode<<Layout>>("return { window = Rect(10, 20, 640, 480) }")
print(layout.window.max) -- 650, 500, 0

layout.window = Rect(vector.create(0, 0, 0), vector.create(800, 600, 0))
print(luwon.encode(layout)) -- return { window = Rect(0, 0, 800, 600) }
```

When `__todata` returns a single table, the file holds the braces form and `__fromdata` gets that table back:

```luwu
class Duration implements luwon.data
    public seconds: number

    -- luwon.encode writes the table this returns as `Duration { minutes = 2, seconds = 30 }`
    public function __todata(self)
        return {
            minutes = self.seconds // 60,
            seconds = self.seconds % 60,
        }
    end

    -- reader:decode calls this with the table between the braces and uses the object it returns
    public function __fromdata(parts: { minutes: number, seconds: number }): Duration
        return Duration { seconds = parts.minutes * 60 + parts.seconds }
    end
end
```

Both are optional.

@luau/global/luwon.decode.documentation:
Reads a data file's text and returns its value.

```luwu
const manifest = luwon.decode<<Manifest>>(text)
```

The type argument says what you expect back. The file isn't checked against it.

A class call like `Point(1, 2)` comes back as a `luwon.tagged`. Use a `luwon.reader` to get
real objects.

Raises an error with the line number when the text isn't a valid data file.

@luau/global/luwon.encode.documentation:
Writes a value as a data file's text.

A value that came from a data file is written back into that file. Only what changed is rewritten,
and comments, consts and layout stay as they were. A new dependency goes into `const dependencies`
and the `return` keeps saying `dependencies`.

Anything else is written fresh.

An object is written as its class call, like `Point(1, 2)`. A class that implements
`luwon.data` can choose what goes in the call with `__todata`.

Raises an error for what a data file can't hold, like a function or a table that contains itself.

@luau/global/luwon.reader.documentation:
Makes a reader that builds the classes you give it.

```luwu
const reader = luwon.reader({ Color, Point })
const theme = reader:decode<<Theme>>(text)
print(class.isinstance(theme.accent, Color)) -- true
```

A reader can't hold two classes with the same name because a data file names classes by name. A
call to a class the reader doesn't have comes back as a `luwon.tagged`.

A class with methods or its own `__init` has to implement `luwon.data` to go in a reader.

@luau/global/luwon.reader/params/0.documentation: The classes data files may build.

@luau/global/luwon.setcomments.documentation:
Sets the comments of `t[key]`. `luwon.encode` writes them.

```luwu
luwon.setcomments(manifest, "name", {
    above = { "the registry's name" },
    after = "lowercase",
})
```

`--` is added for you. It also works on a table you built yourself, unless it has a metatable of
its own.

@luau/global/luwon.setcomments/params/2.documentation: `{ above = { string }?, after = string? }`. What you leave out is removed.

@luau/global/luwon.source.documentation:
Returns the text of the file `t` came from, when `t` is the table the file returned. It doesn't
change when you edit `t`.

@luau/global/luwon.source/params/0.documentation: The table a data file returned.

@luau/global/luwon.tagged.documentation:
A class call from a data file, kept as its name and arguments.

```luwu
const theme = luwon.decode("return { origin = Point(1, 2) }")
print(theme.origin.name) -- "Point"
print(theme.origin.args) -- { 1, 2 }
```

`args` is what the call holds: `Point(1, 2)` gives `{ 1, 2 }` and `Size { width = 3 }` gives
`{ { width = 3 } }`.

`luwon.encode` writes it back as the call it holds now. A `luwon.reader` with the class gives you a
real object instead.

@luau/global/require.documentation:
Imports the module at `path`, returning what the module returned. Require paths use require-by-string syntax, which is described below.

```luwu
-- sibling of the requiring module/file.
const utils = require("./utils")
-- sibling of the parent of the requiring file/module.
const doc = require("../doc")
-- `@packages` is a require alias.
const html = require("@packages/html")
-- `@self` is a hardcoded alias only visible in `init` modules.
const li = require("@self/li")
```
On the filesystem, the term 'module' is mostly synonymous with 'file'. The term 'require-by-string module' may refer to either a file or
a folder with a file named `init.luau`.

### Caching

Requires are cached. The first time a module's required in your codebase, all top-level code in the module will be evaluated.
Subsequent requires to the same module will return the cached value without re-evaluating the entire module. This allows modules
to be used to keep track of state between multiple files in a codebase.

### Require-By-String syntax

Luwu uses Luau's require-by-string syntax for module paths.

Assume you have the following directory structure:

```
project/
├── .luaurc
├── utils/
│   ├── list.luau
│   └── html/
│       ├── elements.luau
│       ├── serde.luau
│       └── init.luau
└── src/
    ├── parse_html.luau
    └── main.luau
```

- To reach `parse_html.luau` from `main.luau`, use `require("./parse_html")`.
- To reach `list.luau` from `main.luau` via relative path, use `require("../utils/list")`
- To reach `html` from `parse_html.luau`, use `require("../utils/html")`. This is allowed because you can directly require a directory if it contains a file named `init.luau`.
- To reach `elements.luau` from `init.luau`, use `require("@self/elements)`. You need `@self` here because `init.luau` is treated *as* its enclosing directory.
- To reach `list.luau` from `html/init.luau`, use `require("./list")`.
- To reach `elements.luau` from `serde.luau`, use `require("./elements")`.

If `.luaurc` defines a require alias `"utils": "./utils"`:
- To reach `list.luau` from `main.luau`, use `require("@utils/list)`
- To reach `html` from `parse_html.luau`, use `require("@utils/html)`

Keep in mind that not all embedders may support the full require-by-string specification, but relative requires and require-by-alias are typically supported.
Require aliases that depend on other require aliases are in the spec but not yet commonly supported.

On the filesystem, you can define your own require aliases by making a `.luaurc` (jsonc-syntax) or `.config.luau` file.
Keep in mind some require aliases may be hardcoded by the embedder and cannot be overriden: for example, in *seal*,
`@std` and `@interop` are hardcoded aliases.

@luau/global/require/params/0.documentation: The require-by-string path of the module you want to require. These should start with `.`, `..`, or `@`.

@luau/global/require/returns/0.documentation: The value the module returned; this may be a cached value.

@luau/global/typeof.documentation:
Returns `value`'s embedder-defined or primitive type tag as a string.

On primitives, this is generally the same string you get with `type`, except for `userdata` and `integer`.
- For userdata (extern types), this returns the `__type` metafield which can be customized by the embedder.
- For integers, this returns the specific integer representation: `type(19u16) == "integer"; typeof(19u16) == "u16"`.

In the type system, you can use `typeof` to narrow on extern types:

```luwu
const t: number | Duration = get_dur()
if typeof(t) == "Duration" then
    -- typechecker refines t to Duration here, no type error
    print(t:display())
else
    -- typechecker knows t is a number here
    print(`{t} seconds`)
end
```

@luau/global/typeof/params/0.documentation: The value to get the typeof tag of.

@luau/global/typeof/returns/0.documentation: The typeof tag of the value
